frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Italy and other European buyers remain dependent on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies, creating bargaining leverage but also pressure for predictable pricing and expanded investment.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya raises border-security costs and complicates Algeria's effort to preserve strategic autonomy without deeper external security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: External financing exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked lending, Western oil majors, and commodity traders retain major influence over Angola's fiscal and infrastructure space despite efforts to renegotiate debt and improve state control.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: US and European backing for the Lobito Corridor increases Angola's strategic value while intensifying competition over access to Congolese and Zambian critical minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border disruption
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger and broader Sahel sanctions dynamics continue to threaten trade through the Port of Cotonou and expose Benin to retaliatory border and transit restrictions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign port influence
frictionVectors.details: International operators, lenders, and regional trading networks remain important to port modernization and logistics, limiting purely national control over critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers partnership tension
frictionVectors.details: Botswana's push for a larger share of diamond value and stronger control over marketing is straining its long-standing partnership with De Beers.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are showing greater interest in Botswana's copper, nickel, and other minerals, creating opportunities while testing regulatory capacity and local-beneficiation ambitions.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta's reliance on Russian security support increases external influence over strategic policy while offering limited guarantees for restoring secure access to mining zones.

frictionVectors.title: Gold smuggling and insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent activity and informal cross-border trading divert gold revenues from the state, undermining efforts to nationalize oversight and expand domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: DRC Border and Rebel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Burundi’s security posture remains tied to instability in eastern DRC, where armed-group activity and competing regional interventions threaten trade routes and border control.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Bargaining Gap
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control over nickel and rare-earth development, but limited capital and infrastructure leave substantial leverage with foreign investors and regional transport networks.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde’s ports and maritime domain attract interest from the United States, Europe, China, and other partners, creating pressure to balance security access with sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Water Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The islands remain dependent on imported fuel, desalination, and external infrastructure finance, limiting resilience despite relatively strong governance and diversified partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cameroon’s control of export corridors, including the Chad-Cameroon pipeline and Kribi port, generates strategic leverage but also leaves revenue and infrastructure vulnerable to foreign operators and financing terms.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Sahel Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside Boko Haram activity in the Far North, constrains state access to land, agricultural resources, and transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Security partnerships linked to Russia provide regime protection while increasing scrutiny over opaque access to gold, diamonds, and other extractive sites outside transparent state regulation.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Weak control over roads and borders enables armed groups and cross-border traders to capture value, while dependence on external security providers limits independent state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Chad-Cameroon Pipeline Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s oil revenues depend on a foreign-linked pipeline and export system, leaving sovereign fiscal control exposed to operator influence, transit risks, and volatile global prices.

frictionVectors.title: Post-French Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The reduction of France’s military role is widening competition among regional, Russian, and Western partners for security access, while instability around Sudan and Libya strains Chad’s borders.

highlights: Gulf and Indian Ocean partners expand engagement

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a core territorial dispute and limiting Comoros' effective authority over surrounding maritime space. Migration pressures keep relations politically charged.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on diaspora remittances and external partners for infrastructure and budget support, leaving development priorities vulnerable to outside political leverage.

frictionVectors.title: M23, Rwanda, and eastern corridors
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in North Kivu and South Kivu continues to weaken Kinshasa's control over territory, border trade, and mining zones. Rwanda-linked security dynamics and regional mediation remain decisive external variables.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain major influence across mining, processing, and infrastructure, while the United States and Europe seek alternative critical-mineral partnerships. Weak governance limits the state's ability to capture full value from its resources.

highlights: Oil revenue still anchors state power

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state remains highly dependent on oil exports and foreign technical capital, exposing fiscal sovereignty to price cycles and production-sharing arrangements dominated by international operators.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and industrial projects provide essential connectivity but deepen dependence on external finance and commodity-linked repayment structures. France and other partners remain influential in energy and finance.

highlights: Cocoa and hydrocarbons drive strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire remains a leading cocoa producer but captures limited downstream value relative to multinational traders and processors. Regulatory efforts to raise farmer incomes face market and climate constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Port and energy competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and expanding gas and power infrastructure attract French, Chinese, Gulf, and other investors. This strengthens national capacity while creating long-term exposure to foreign capital and operating expertise.

highlights: Strategic bases outweigh domestic resource depth
Ports remain the core sovereignty asset

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position through U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities, but the resulting security dependence narrows strategic autonomy and raises escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: Port debt and Ethiopian dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port and logistics infrastructure is vital to Ethiopia's trade and Djibouti's revenues, yet external financing and Chinese-linked assets constrain domestic control. Any Ethiopia-Djibouti tension or debt stress could quickly affect national security.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and major Gulf investments are stabilizing Egypt's finances but increase outside influence over strategic assets and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains Egypt's principal long-term resource-security risk, especially during periods of drought or low Nile flows.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Falling hydrocarbon output and limited economic diversification leave the state vulnerable to foreign operators, volatile prices, and declining fiscal space.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external firms remain important to infrastructure and energy development, creating leverage over strategic facilities and future gas projects.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline gives it strategic leverage amid Red Sea competition, but pressure from Gulf states, Ethiopia, and wider maritime security interests could constrain policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard currency but expose Eritrea to foreign concessionaires, sanctions risk, and limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Trade and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African markets, electricity networks, and transport corridors, limiting room for independent resource and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Fiscal and Investment Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Constrained public finances and dependence on external investors slow industrial diversification and leave strategic projects vulnerable to donor and regional conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's control over electricity generation and water infrastructure while sustaining acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Infrastructure and Debt
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and multilateral financing remains important for transport and energy, creating external leverage as Ethiopia manages debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages.

highlights: Mining and oil leverage being renegotiated

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic commodities
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is seeking greater state participation and local value addition in manganese and oil, but Chinese, French and other foreign firms remain central to capital, technology and export access.

frictionVectors.title: Transgabon railway vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The railway is vital for manganese exports and domestic connectivity, yet aging infrastructure and dependence on external financing limit Libreville's operational autonomy.

highlights: Senegal remains the decisive external partner

frictionVectors.title: Foreign pressure on fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign-linked fleets continues to test enforcement capacity and public trust, while the state captures limited value from maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia trade and border dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia's economy relies heavily on transit through Senegal and regional supply chains, leaving customs policy, border closures and transport bottlenecks highly consequential.

highlights: Debt and illegal mining constrain room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector state intervention
frictionVectors.details: Accra is expanding state oversight of gold purchasing and formalization to retain more export value, but smuggling networks and foreign-linked refining and trading channels remain influential.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and water security
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal mining, including operations involving foreign nationals and equipment, is degrading rivers and farmland while challenging the government's ability to enforce resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project promises major revenues and infrastructure, but rail, port and financing arrangements give foreign consortia substantial influence over Guinea's export architecture.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite bargaining and political transition
frictionVectors.details: The junta is using permits, local-processing demands and contract reviews to increase state leverage, while opaque governance and delayed political normalization raise investor and sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture much of the value from Guinea-Bissau's dominant export, while weak regulation and limited domestic processing reduce state bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Port, narcotics and maritime insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's weak institutions and limited maritime surveillance create openings for transnational trafficking networks and foreign security influence, complicating control of ports and coastal resources.

frictionVectors.title: Mombasa and Lamu Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing Chinese-built and financed infrastructure with Gulf, Western, and regional investment around its ports and transport corridors. Debt servicing and project profitability limit Nairobi's room to dictate terms.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Energy Financing
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital is increasingly important for geothermal expansion, grid modernization, and mineral development. The government is seeking stronger local benefits while avoiding contracts that could reproduce dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: South Africa remains the dominant buyer, financier, and infrastructure partner for Lesotho's strategic water exports. Delays, compensation disputes, and unequal bargaining power constrain Maseru's control over its most valuable resource.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Industrial Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's apparel sector depends heavily on external buyers, imported inputs, and preferential trade access. Shifts in global sourcing or U.S. trade policy can rapidly affect employment and fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Rail Access
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore expansion is strengthening export revenues but leaves Liberia dependent on foreign operators for capital, rail logistics, and port access. Concession terms and local-content demands remain central sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Energy and Maritime Security
frictionVectors.details: Liberia is seeking investment in offshore hydrocarbons and maritime infrastructure while protecting its shipping-registration and coastal interests. Limited state capacity creates exposure to external commercial and security actors.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Control of Oil Institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest control over production, export terminals, budgets, and the central bank. Oil remains the principal source of state revenue but also the main engine of political fragmentation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, Egypt, the UAE, and European states retain overlapping security and energy interests in Libya. External backing reduces incentives for a unified national settlement and complicates independent resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Mineral Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining operations provide export earnings but leave Madagascar reliant on foreign capital, imported technology, and global commodity prices. Fiscal returns, environmental impacts, and community compensation remain contested.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: External powers and multinational firms are increasing interest in Madagascar's graphite, nickel, cobalt, and strategic ports. Antananarivo is trying to diversify partners while preventing infrastructure and mineral contracts from eroding national control.

frictionVectors.title: MINING LICENSE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is courting foreign capital for uranium, graphite and rare-earth projects, but limited domestic financing and technical capacity reduce state leverage over concessions.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND INPUT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Fuel, fertilizer and electricity shortages expose Malawi to external price shocks and donor-linked financing conditions, constraining sovereign development choices.

highlights: Junta tightens control over gold and strategic partnerships
Russian security ties substitute for Western support

frictionVectors.title: GOLD RESOURCE NATIONALISM
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is revising mining arrangements and demanding a larger public share of gold revenues, generating friction with multinational operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel provides political cover but increases exposure to opaque contracting, civilian-risk allegations and strategic dependence on Moscow.

highlights: Gas exports broaden leverage beyond iron ore
Nouakchott balances Europe, Gulf and Chinese capital

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE GAS CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project can strengthen public finances, but foreign operators and cross-border arrangements with Senegal limit Mauritania's unilateral control over infrastructure and revenues.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCENTRATION
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore remains central to exports, leaving the state exposed to external commodity cycles and the bargaining power of foreign mining and logistics partners.

highlights: Blue-economy and renewables agenda gains weight

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius sits near increasingly contested Indian Ocean sea lanes and must balance security, port and infrastructure ties with India, China and Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY IMPORT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fossil fuels remains a structural vulnerability, although renewable deployment and regional connectivity could gradually improve national resilience.

highlights: Phosphate and green-industry strategy strengthens leverage

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses investment and infrastructure in Western Sahara to reinforce its sovereignty claim, while Algeria, the Polisario Front and some international actors continue to contest the political and legal framework.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL CAPITAL BALANCING
frictionVectors.details: Large projects depend on European, Gulf, Chinese and U.S. finance, requiring Rabat to manage competing partners without surrendering control over ports, energy networks or strategic industries.

highlights: Maputo Balances Gulf and Western Capital

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence continues to threaten LNG infrastructure and constrain state access to gas-rich northern districts. Foreign security assistance remains central to protecting strategic projects.

frictionVectors.title: External LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders retain substantial leverage over LNG development, limiting Mozambique's near-term control over revenue timing and project terms.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Critical-Mineral Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms dominate much of the capital-intensive uranium and mineral sector, while Windhoek seeks greater local processing, fiscal returns, and strategic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Financing
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale hydrogen projects depend on European and other external finance, creating opportunities for development but risks of foreign control over infrastructure and export chains.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium Contract Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is pressing to renegotiate foreign uranium interests and increase national control, raising legal, operational, and diplomatic risks.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Export Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Oil-export infrastructure depends on regional transit and external operators, leaving Niger exposed to border insecurity, sanctions pressure, and political disputes with neighbors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil-Capital Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain important to deepwater investment and technical capacity, while production losses and contract uncertainty constrain Nigeria's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Grid Weakness
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, vandalism, and unreliable electricity infrastructure reduce the state's effective control of energy assets and divert revenue from public development.

frictionVectors.title: Great Lakes Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's mineral-trading and regional security posture attract international scrutiny over supply-chain traceability and alleged links to conflict minerals from eastern DRC.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The government retains strong policy control, but dependence on external aid, investors, and security partnerships creates vulnerability to diplomatic conditionality.

highlights: Gulf of Guinea security cooperation deepens

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE LICENSING UNCERTAINTY
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain interested in offshore blocks, but limited discoveries and weak state capacity constrain São Tomé and Príncipe’s bargaining power. Oil expectations continue to shape fiscal planning despite uncertain commercial viability.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME CAPACITY GAP
frictionVectors.details: The country depends on external partners for maritime surveillance, fisheries enforcement, and Gulf of Guinea security. This protects trade routes but leaves strategic control over surrounding waters limited.

highlights: Oil and gas revenue enters a contested phase

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACT RESET
frictionVectors.details: Dakar is seeking greater transparency and national participation in oil and gas projects, creating friction with established foreign operators and lenders. Production offers fiscal upside but also exposes Senegal to arbitration, debt, and revenue-management risks.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCING PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Large transport and energy projects remain dependent on foreign capital, contractors, and imported technology. Debt constraints may narrow the government’s ability to convert strategic infrastructure into fully sovereign assets.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES ACCESS AND ENFORCEMENT
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from foreign fishing access and processing investment but must balance licensing revenue against overfishing and conservation concerns. Limited patrol capacity keeps enforcement reliant on outside support.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN STRATEGIC COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: India, China, Gulf states, and Western partners compete for port, maritime-security, and connectivity influence. Victoria seeks to preserve strategic autonomy while avoiding dependence on any single partner.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND RUTILE BARGAINING
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining operations generate exports and jobs but leave Sierra Leone exposed to commodity cycles, infrastructure bottlenecks, and disputes over taxation and local value addition. The state’s negotiating leverage is constrained by its need for investment and foreign exchange.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Mining competitiveness depends on externally financed roads, ports, energy, and logistics systems. Chinese and other foreign contractors are influential, raising concerns about procurement transparency and long-term control of strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Turkey and Gulf actors shape maritime strategy

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE RESOURCE ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Somalia’s offshore oil ambitions attract foreign operators and political competition while federal-state disputes complicate licensing and revenue sharing. Weak regulatory capacity increases the risk that future resource gains will be captured by external firms or domestic elites.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, BASES, AND RED SEA RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: Foreign security and infrastructure partnerships, especially involving Turkey and Gulf actors, provide essential support but deepen competition over ports and maritime access. Somalia gains capacity while risking fragmented control over strategic coastal assets.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity and rail-port constraints weaken South Africa's ability to capture value from minerals. Foreign capital remains important in power, mining, and infrastructure, creating leverage over strategic sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-processing competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-mineral supply chains. Pretoria is seeking downstream processing without fully alienating external investors.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan pipeline dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving revenues vulnerable to sabotage, political bargaining, and transit disruption. This sharply limits Juba's economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Regional actors and international firms compete for influence around oil, roads, and security assistance while domestic elites control much of the rent distribution. Weak institutions make transparent resource management difficult.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and oil corridors
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed authorities and foreign networks are contesting gold production, export routes, and oil infrastructure. Resource revenues increasingly sustain wartime actors rather than national reconstruction.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics leverage
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and Red Sea access has become strategically important to Gulf, Russian, Egyptian, and other external interests. Infrastructure and security partnerships risk entrenching fragmented sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: LNG contract sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over large-scale offshore gas development place Tanzania between demands for domestic value addition and pressure from international energy companies for predictable terms. Delays preserve bargaining room but defer revenue and infrastructure gains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and other external investors are competing around ports, railways, and logistics links serving the interior. Dar es Salaam is expanding strategic autonomy, but financing terms and operating concessions remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a key commercial and transshipment asset, attracting external operators and financing while exposing Togo to competition among Gulf, Chinese, European, and regional interests. Security demands from the Sahel add pressure on northern transport links.

frictionVectors.title: Limited mineral sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control over phosphate resources but captures limited value beyond extraction and basic processing. Dependence on foreign technology, capital, and export markets constrains domestic leverage.

highlights: Energy ties pivot toward Algeria and Italy

frictionVectors.title: MIGRATION-FINANCE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: European funding and cooperation on migration remain important sources of leverage, while Tunisia resists political conditionality and faces persistent fiscal pressure.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY IMPORT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported gas and constrained power infrastructure leaves Tunisia exposed to Algerian supply terms, Italian connectivity priorities, and volatile external financing.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP EXTERNAL CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline and upstream projects tie Uganda's future export revenues to foreign operators, lenders, and transit arrangements through Tanzania, limiting near-term domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external financing has expanded transport and energy capacity, but repayment obligations and project terms constrain fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: COPPER VALUE-CHAIN CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking more processing, transparent contracts, and stronger state participation, but foreign mining firms still dominate capital, technology, and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-LED POLICY CONSTRAINT
frictionVectors.details: Official restructuring has eased immediate pressure, yet creditor conditions and reliance on multilateral support continue to shape infrastructure and resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: LITHIUM AND MINERAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Export controls and local-processing ambitions seek greater sovereign capture, but Chinese and other foreign investors retain major influence over mining finance, technology, and offtake.

frictionVectors.title: ELECTRICITY INFRASTRUCTURE CRISIS
frictionVectors.details: Chronic generation shortfalls force reliance on imports and private solutions, weakening domestic industrial capacity and increasing exposure to regional power suppliers.
